record.paper_title: New results and open problems on subgraph centrality
record.original_question: Let G be a graph, let i and j be two vertices of G, and let I be the set of positive real numbers β for which the two vertices are β-subgraph equivalent, meaning that their subgraph centralities agree: [e^{βA}]_{ii} = [e^{βA}]_{jj}, where A is the adjacency matrix of G. The paper proves that if I has an accumulation point then i and j are cospectral and in fact I = R_+. Is some weaker finiteness hypothesis already enough? More precisely, if I is finite, can one still conclude that i and j are cospectral under additional assumptions, and is there any condition on the cardinality M = |I| that forces this conclusion?

evidence.quote: It is natural to ask if this result can be improved. For example, is it still true if I is finite? Is there any condition on M = |I|, the cardinality of I, under which the result holds?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph with adjacency matrix $A$, and let $i,j$ be two vertices of $G$. For $\beta>0$, the $\beta$-subgraph centrality of a vertex $k$ is defined as $[e^{\beta A}]_{kk}$, the $(k,k)$-entry of the matrix exponential $e^{\beta A}=\sum_{n\ge 0}\beta^n A^n/n!$. We say that $i$ and $j$ are $\beta$-subgraph equivalent if $[e^{\beta A}]_{ii}=[e^{\beta A}]_{jj}$. The vertices $i$ and $j$ are called cospectral if the characteristic polynomials of the principal submatrices of $A$ obtained by deleting the row and column indexed by $i$ and by $j$ coincide (equivalently, $[A^n]_{ii}=[A^n]_{jj}$ for every $n\ge 0$).

Let
$$I=I(i,j)=\{\beta\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}:[e^{\beta A}]_{ii}=[e^{\beta A}]_{jj}\}.$$
It is known that if $I$ has an accumulation point in $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$, then $i$ and $j$ are cospectral and in fact $I=\mathbb{R}_{>0}$.

Determine whether a strictly weaker finiteness hypothesis suffices. Specifically:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Suppose $I$ is a finite, nonempty set. Under what additional structural hypotheses on $G$ (or on $i,j$) can one conclude that $i$ and $j$ are cospectral?
\item Is there an integer $M_0$, or a function $M_0=M_0(G)$, such that whenever the cardinality $|I|\ge M_0$, the vertices $i$ and $j$ must be cospectral?
\end{enumerate}
artifact.status_search_result: Web searches surface the proof that two vertices with equal β-subgraph centrality for an algebraic β (or for a set with an accumulation point) must be cospectral, settling Estrada's conjecture and a generalization due to Kloster–Král–Sullivan. However, no result addresses the case of a merely finite β-equivalence set or provides a cardinality threshold |I|=M forcing cospectrality. The question therefore appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Vertex distinction with subgraph centrality: A proof of Estrada's conjecture and some generalizations
status_evidence.snippet: For algebraic β, two vertices with equal β-subgraph centrality are necessarily cospectral; settles Estrada's conjecture and a generalization due to Kloster, Král and Sullivan.
status_evidence.claim: Existing literature handles the case of accumulation points / algebraic β but does not address the finite-cardinality question.

status_evidence.title: Constructing Cospectral Vertices Through Orbits of Subgraphs
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work on constructing cospectral vertices via subgraph orbits, without addressing thresholds on |I| for β-equivalence implying cospectrality.
status_evidence.claim: No subsequent paper found that resolves the finite-I version of the question.
